newsitem.title: USA: Bulgaria, Bolivia on US copyright-rules watch list.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria, Bolivia on US copyright-rules watch list.

text.p: Bolivia and Bulgaria were put on a "watch list" that will put more U.S. pressure on them to improve their protection of intellectual property rights, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Wednesday.
As a result of "out of cycle" reviews, Barschefsky said Paraguay would remain on the watch list and South Africa would stay off the list.
A decision on Greece, now on the list, was deferred until mid-December.

Under so-called "special 301" provisions of U.S. trade law, the trade representative's office reports at least once a year on nations that fail to protect copyrights, patents, trademarks and other forms of intellectual property rights.
Nations posing the greatest problems are put on a "watch list" or "priority watch list" and monitored for progress.

"Our copyright industries -- computer software, film, television, book publishing and music -- represent five percent of gross domestic product, more than three million jobs and a $400 billion international marketplace," Barshefksy said.
Bulgaria was put on the watch list because of reports of pirate production of CDs and CD-ROMs for sale in Europe.
Bolivia was placed on the watch list for failing to adequately combat copyright piracy, especially in computer software and for not improving copyright protection.

Paraguay has taken steps to improve copyright and trademark protection, but Barshefsky expressed concern that Paraguay was a gateway for illegal shipment of Asian products. While Paraguay was not elevated to the priority watch list, Barshefsky said "significant, meaningul progress" was vital before the April annual review.

South Africa was provisionally taken off the watch list in April. Barshefsky said a recent South African court decision should provide the basis for more effective protection of well-known trademarks.

A decison on Greece's status was deferred until mid-December following government initiation of action to countermand broadcast piracy. In addition, Barshefsky noted that Greece recently concluded national elections. In the interim, she said, Greece was expected to vigorously apply its mass media law and to act against TV stations that make unauthorized broadcasts of movies and other programs.
